items.title: 163 clinical directions were never registered
items.blocker: POS-001 detects clinical direction from a list of imperative openers. The list was built from directive prose, so Assess, Avoid and Prefer were in it and Weigh, Stage, Correct, Offer and Confirm were not. A dry run across every professional page found 163 directions on 101 pages that had never reached the position register, among them 'Stage the corner before any cruciate reconstruction in a knee with lateral findings' and 'Correct varus alignment where it would load a corner reconstruction'. Both are clinical direction and both had been live for days.
items.needed: Nothing in the tool. The verb list was extended, the register re-extracted and 7 tests added. With decision 019's consultation verbs the unsigned total rose from 976 to 1,295, which is a correction to the count rather than new exposure: the advice was always on the page and simply not on the list anybody is asked to sign. Found only because the consultant tier rewrite under decision 018 moved into weighing language the detector could not see.

items.title: POSITION_VERBS is a verb list, and it was extended twice in one day
items.blocker: POS-001 detects clinical direction from a list of imperative openers. Decision 018 extended it for weighing verbs and decision 019 extended it again for consultation verbs, both times because prose in a register the list had never seen went undetected. A list that needs extending whenever the writing changes register is keeping pace rather than leading, and the next new register will find the same gap.
items.needed: No replacement is proposed, because the obvious alternatives are worse. A general imperative parser over-collects far more than the list does, and a model-based detector is not deterministic and cannot sit in a gate that has to give the same answer twice. Flagged so the next person does not assume it went unnoticed.

items.blocker: Functional Anatomy and Motion. Ten pages on the six degrees of freedom, the six motions taken one at a time, how they couple, and stability through the arc. Three tiers on every page, medical student to FRCS, and no junior or patient tier: the architecture does not ask for one here. The chapter orients rather than apportions, because per ligament restraint belongs to chapters 3.7 to 3.11 and surface motion to 3.3.
items.needed: Consultant review. Nothing in the chapter is held: the chapter's ten pages are its whole plan.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.3
items.state: All 14 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: Knee Kinematics, the largest chapter in Section 3 so far. Eight pages on the mechanics: how motion is described, roll and glide, the two chains, the screw home mechanism and its reverse, the instant centre of rotation, and how all of it changes through flexion. Six more on the activities: walking, running, squatting, stairs, landing and cutting. Three tiers on every page, medical student to FRCS.
items.needed: Consultant review. Kinetics is handed to chapter 3.4, gait pathology to 3.14 and 4.4, and sport specific application to 3.15, all by the architecture's own must_not_cover list rather than by choice.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.4
items.state: All 10 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: Knee Kinetics, the other half of chapter 3.3. Ten pages on forces and moments: what kinetics is, the ground reaction force, joint reaction forces, lever arms, moments and their external and internal halves, energy absorption, force transmission and shock absorption. Three tiers on every page, medical student to FRCS.
items.needed: Consultant review. The chapter carries more measurements than any other in Section 3, because a kinetic claim without a magnitude says nothing, and every one of them is written from standard teaching. Contact area and stress are handed to 3.5.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.5
items.state: All 10 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: Tibiofemoral Contact Mechanics, where chapters 3.3 and 3.4 arrive. Four pages on the normal state: contact areas, contact pressures, load distribution and the effect of flexion. Three on what changes it: meniscal loss, malalignment and body mass. Three on the knee after an event: cruciate injury, meniscectomy and osteotomy. Three tiers on every page.
items.needed: Consultant review, and this chapter needs it most. Every page turns on the distinction between force and stress, and almost every figure in it is a cadaveric contact measurement quoted from memory. If the area and pressure numbers are wrong, the mechanical argument of three chapters is wrong with them.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.6
items.state: All 14 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: Meniscal Biomechanics, where four chapters arrive. Eight pages on the structure and its functions: the five roles, hoop stress, the two fibre systems, load sharing, damping, lubrication and proprioception. Three on the roots and what fails: root biomechanics, extrusion, root tears. Three on the rest: radial tears, repair constructs and transplantation. The last two carry a fellowship tier, which the architecture asks for and no other page in Section 3 has.
items.needed: Consultant review by someone who repairs menisci. Every mechanical statement in the chapter rests on hoop tension, and the chapter says so on its first substantive page. If that framing is overstated anywhere, fourteen pages are wrong together. Tear classification is handed to chapters 6.28 to 6.43 and MRI appearances to 5.6.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.7
items.state: All 20 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: ACL Biomechanics, the largest chapter in Section 3 and the most referenced from elsewhere in it. Eight pages on what the ligament does, two on how the knee behaves without it, four on what loads it, one on injury mechanism, one on sex differences, and five on grafts and the reconstructed construct. The last five carry a fellowship tier.
items.needed: Consultant review by a knee surgeon who reconstructs. The chapter carries the graft property figures, the strain figures and the apportionment percentages, all from memory, and they are the numbers trainees will quote. 3.7.15 on sex differences needs reading for tone as well as accuracy: it states a rate difference, separates group level findings from individual prediction, and says the modifiable factors are the trainable ones.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.8
items.state: All 10 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: PCL Biomechanics. Six pages on function and behaviour, one on gait, three on reconstruction, the last three with a fellowship tier. The chapter is shaped differently from the anterior cruciate's because the ligament is: stronger, injured less often, partly healing, and reconstructed less successfully, and each of those four facts is mechanical.
items.needed: Consultant review. Two things in it need checking by someone who does these operations: the bundle arrangement is the reverse of the anterior cruciate's and the chapter says so repeatedly, and the step off figures and grading thresholds are quoted from memory. The tensioning angle and the instruction to reduce the sag before fixation are the practical claims most worth confirming.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.9
items.state: All 10 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: Medial Knee Biomechanics. Two pages on what the side does, four on the individual structures, one on the corner as a unit, one on the rotatory instability pattern, one on the reconstruction and one on the combined injury. 3.9.8 carries a fellowship tier.
items.needed: Consultant review. The chapter's organising claim is that the medial side divides its work by flexion angle, with the superficial ligament primary at 20 to 30 degrees and the posteromedial corner taking over near extension. Two practical claims most worth confirming: the two tibial attachments of the superficial ligament behaving differently, and the tensioning angles given for the two limbs of a medial reconstruction.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.10
items.state: All 9 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: Lateral Knee Biomechanics, the mirror of 3.9 and not a symmetrical one. Two pages on what the side does, three on the structures, one on the corner as a unit, one on the mechanics behind the dial test, one on reconstruction and one on the combined injury. 3.10.8 carries a fellowship tier.
items.needed: Consultant review by someone who reconstructs corners. The three component reconstruction, the tensioning position, and the claim that a missed corner injury is a leading cause of graft failure on both cruciates are the statements that carry the most weight. The dial test page states the mechanics and hands the technique to 4.13, which is worth checking for the boundary as well as the content.

items.title: Section 3 Biomechanics Academy, chapter 3.11
items.state: All 9 pages written, style gate passed, awaiting review
items.blocker: Anterolateral Complex Biomechanics, the chapter where the anatomy is still argued over. Three pages on the structures, two on what they control, one on the Segond lesion as evidence of an attachment, one on the tenodesis, one on the combined reconstruction and one on the controversies. Four pages carry a fellowship tier and 3.11.9 is the first page in Section 3 to carry a consultant tier.
items.needed: Consultant review by an ACL surgeon who uses lateral augmentation. The pages that carry the most weight are 3.11.3, which separates the naming question from the functional one, 3.11.7, where the clinical evidence is strongest and the anatomical rationale weakest, and 3.11.9, which sets out two defensible consultant positions rather than one answer. The indication threshold for augmentation is the single statement most likely to be contested.
